systems.name: Skeletal
systems.tagline: The living frame — support, shape and armor.

organs.name: Skull
organs.function: A bony helmet that protects the brain and shapes the face.
facts: It is made of 22 bones locked together by puzzle-like joints called sutures.
The lower jaw is the only skull bone that moves freely.
A baby's skull bones finish growing together at around 18 months.

organs.name: Rib cage
organs.function: A cage of ribs that shields the heart and lungs and helps breathing.
facts: Twelve pairs of ribs curve from the spine to the front of the chest.
Muscles between the ribs lift the chest when you breathe in.
The lowest two pairs float — they attach only at the back.

organs.name: Spine
organs.function: A stack of 33 bones that holds you upright and protects the spinal cord.
facts: Squishy cushions between the bones let you bend and twist.
Seen from the side it forms a gentle S curve.
You are a few millimetres taller in the morning, when the cushions are most relaxed.

organs.name: Pelvis
organs.function: A bowl of bone at the hip that carries the body's weight down to the legs.
facts: It cradles the digestive organs like a basket.
The leg bones plug into sockets on each side of the pelvis.
Its wide, flat shape is part of what makes human walking efficient.

systems.name: Circulatory
systems.tagline: The delivery loop — blood, pumped everywhere.

organs.name: Heart
organs.function: A muscle pump, about the size of your fist, that pushes blood around the body.
facts: It beats around 100,000 times a day without taking a rest.
Its right side pumps blood to the lungs; its left side pumps to the rest of the body.
One-way doors called valves keep blood from flowing backwards.

organs.name: Arteries
organs.function: Thick-walled tubes that carry blood away from the heart.
facts: The aorta, the biggest artery, is as wide as a garden hose.
Artery walls pulse in time with the heartbeat — that's your pulse.
They branch like a tree, ending in vessels thinner than a hair.

organs.name: Veins
organs.function: Tubes that return used blood to the heart.
facts: Veins hold one-way valves so blood cannot slide back down.
Moving muscles squeeze veins and help push blood home.
About two thirds of your blood is stored in the veins at any moment.

systems.name: Respiratory
systems.tagline: The air exchange — oxygen in, carbon dioxide out.

organs.name: Trachea
organs.function: The windpipe: a firm tube that carries air between the throat and the lungs.
facts: Rings of cartilage keep it propped open, like the hose of a vacuum.
A flap called the epiglottis covers it whenever you swallow.
At the bottom it splits into two bronchi, one for each lung.

organs.name: Lungs
organs.function: Two spongy sacs where oxygen moves into the blood and carbon dioxide moves out.
facts: You breathe in and out about 20,000 times a day.
The right lung has three lobes; the left has two, leaving room for the heart.
Breathing out is relaxed — the muscle work happens when you breathe in.

organs.name: Diaphragm
organs.function: A dome-shaped muscle under the lungs that powers breathing.
facts: When it pulls downward the chest gets bigger and air rushes in.
A hiccup is a sudden, surprise squeeze of the diaphragm.
It works with the rib muscles day and night, without you thinking about it.

systems.name: Digestive
systems.tagline: The fuel line — food broken down to nutrients.

organs.name: Esophagus
organs.function: A muscular tube that squeezes food from the mouth down to the stomach.
facts: It moves food in waves — strong enough that you could swallow upside down.
The journey from throat to stomach takes about eight seconds.
A ring of muscle at the bottom keeps the stomach tightly shut.

organs.name: Stomach
organs.function: A stretchy mixing bag where food is broken down by acid and churning.
facts: It can stretch from the size of a fist to the size of a melon.
Stomach acid is strong — a slimy lining protects the walls from it.
Food leaves the stomach as a soup called chyme.

organs.name: Liver
organs.function: The body's chemical factory: it cleans, stores and sends out nutrients.
facts: It is the largest organ inside the body.
It makes bile, a liquid that breaks fat into tiny drops.
Everything the intestines absorb passes through the liver first.

organs.name: Small intestine
organs.function: A long coiled tube where most nutrients pass into the blood.
facts: Uncoiled it is about six metres — roughly three times your height.
Millions of finger-like villi give its surface the texture of a towel.
Food spends three to five hours travelling through it.

organs.name: Large intestine
organs.function: The final stretch: it soaks up water and packs away what is left.
facts: It is shorter but much wider than the small intestine — about 1.5 metres.
Trillions of helpful bacteria live here.
Whatever the body cannot use becomes waste and leaves.

systems.name: Nervous
systems.tagline: The wiring — signals from brain to toes.

organs.name: Brain
organs.function: The control centre: it thinks, remembers and commands the whole body.
facts: It contains about 86 billion nerve cells.
It runs on roughly 20 watts of power — like a dim light bulb.
Some signals between brain cells travel at up to 400 km/h.

organs.name: Spinal cord
organs.function: A thick cable of nerves running from the brain down inside the spine.
facts: It is about 45 centimetres long and as thick as your thumb.
Fast reflexes, like snapping back from something hot, are handled here.
The vertebrae of the spine shield it all the way down.

organs.name: Nerves
organs.function: A wiring network that carries signals between brain, spinal cord and body.
facts: The longest nerve runs from your spine all the way to your big toe.
Nerves tell muscles to move and skin to feel.
Laid end to end, the body's nerves would stretch almost four times around the Earth.
